title: Medical Language and Documentation
summary: Speak and write medicine: roots, abbreviations, notes and presentations.

lessons.title: Medical Word Roots, Prefixes and Suffixes

levels.kid:
Doctors use special long words, but those words are made of little building blocks, like LEGO.

One block tells you the body part. "Cardi" means heart. "Gastr" means tummy. Another block tells you what is happening. "-itis" means swollen and sore. So "gastritis" means a sore, swollen tummy!

Some blocks go at the front. "Tachy" means fast, so "tachycardia" means a fast heartbeat. "Brady" means slow.

Once you know the blocks, you can figure out giant words all by yourself, like a code breaker.
levels.hs:
Medical terms look scary, but most are built from three kinds of parts:
- **Root**: the core meaning, usually a body part. cardi = heart, hepat = liver, nephr = kidney, neur = nerve, oste = bone, derm = skin.
- **Prefix**: goes in front and changes the meaning. hyper- = above/too much, hypo- = below/too little, tachy- = fast, brady- = slow, a-/an- = without.
- **Suffix**: goes at the end and usually tells you the condition or procedure. -itis = inflammation, -ectomy = surgical removal, -ology = study of, -algia = pain, -emia = blood condition, -megaly = enlargement.

A combining vowel, usually "o", glues parts together when the next part starts with a consonant: oste + o + porosis = osteoporosis.

Put it together:
- Hepatitis = liver inflammation.
- Appendectomy = removal of the appendix.
- Hepatomegaly = enlarged liver.
- Bradycardia = slow heart rate.
- Anemia = literally "without blood," meaning too few red blood cells or too little hemoglobin.

Why it matters: thousands of terms stop being memorization and become decoding. If you see "cholecystectomy," you can break it into chole (bile) + cyst (bladder) + ectomy (removal): removing the gallbladder.
levels.college:
Medical terminology is a compositional language drawn mostly from Greek and Latin. Decoding a term means splitting it into prefix, root(s), combining vowel and suffix, then reading the meaning usually from the suffix backward: "gastroenteritis" = inflammation (-itis) of the stomach (gastr) and intestine (enter).

Useful suffix families:
- **Procedures**: -ectomy (excision), -otomy (incision into), -ostomy (creating an opening, e.g. colostomy), -plasty (surgical repair or reshaping), -scopy (visual examination), -centesis (puncture to remove fluid, e.g. thoracentesis), -desis (fusion, e.g. arthrodesis).
- **Conditions**: -itis (inflammation), -osis (abnormal condition or process), -oma (tumor or mass), -pathy (disease), -penia (deficiency, e.g. neutropenia), -philia or -cytosis (increase, e.g. leukocytosis), -rrhea (flow or discharge), -rrhage (bursting forth, e.g. hemorrhage), -plegia (paralysis), -paresis (weakness).

Key prefixes: dys- (abnormal or difficult, dyspnea), poly- (many, polyuria), olig- (few, oliguria), peri- (around, pericarditis), endo- (within), epi- (upon), sub- (below), intra- (inside), hemi- (half, hemiplegia).

Two traps. First, many organs have a Greek root and a Latin root used in different contexts: nephr- (nephrology, nephritis) versus ren- (renal); hepat- versus the rarely used Latin jecur; pneum-/pulmon- for lung. Clinicians say "renal failure" but "nephrotic syndrome." Second, -oma usually means tumor but not always malignant: a lipoma is benign, a hematoma is just a collection of blood, and a granuloma is an inflammatory structure.

Eponyms (Parkinson disease, Bell palsy) cannot be decoded and must be learned, and modern style increasingly drops the possessive.
levels.phd:
Medical vocabulary is a stratified lexicon. Its oldest layer comes from Hippocratic Greek (dyspnea, diarrhea, nephritis); Galen and later Latin writers added anatomical Latin (renal, cerebrum, vertebra); Renaissance anatomists coined Neo-Latin names; and the nineteenth and twentieth centuries produced hybrid neologisms, often mixing Greek and Latin in ways purists dislike ("television" style hybrids such as "hypertension," with Greek hyper- and Latin tensio).

The system is productive: new terms are generated from existing morphemes, which is why a learner who knows a few hundred elements can parse thousands of words. Formal anatomical naming is standardized by Terminologia Anatomica, while diseases are coded in classifications such as ICD and concepts are mapped in ontologies such as SNOMED CT, which link synonyms and allow computers to reason over clinical text.

Semantic drift is a real source of error. "Hysteria" derives from the Greek for uterus, reflecting a discredited theory of disease; "malaria" means "bad air" from the miasma era; "influenza" referenced the influence of the stars. Morphology tells you the origin of a word, not necessarily the current biology.

Some morphemes are polysemous. "-plasty" means surgical shaping, but "-plasia" means growth or formation (hyperplasia, dysplasia, aplasia). "Cyst" can mean bladder (cystitis) or a fluid-filled sac. "Cephal" is head, but "encephal" is brain (inside the head). Hidden ambiguity also exists between similar-sounding terms: ileum (small bowel) and ilium (pelvic bone); perineal and peroneal; hypo- and hyper- differing by one letter.

Corpus studies of clinical notes show that abbreviations, not long Greek words, cause most comprehension failures, which leads naturally into the safety rules practitioners follow.
levels.expert:
On the wards, the vocabulary problem is less about long words and more about speed and safety.

First, precision. Attendings expect you to use the exact term: "dyspnea on exertion" rather than "trouble breathing," "hematemesis" (vomiting blood) versus "hemoptysis" (coughing up blood). Mixing those two sends the workup to the wrong organ system: GI bleed versus lung or airway. Likewise "-paresis" (weakness) is not "-plegia" (complete paralysis), and in neurology the difference changes localization and prognosis.

Second, abbreviations. Many hospitals and The Joint Commission maintain a "Do Not Use" list because some abbreviations have caused fatal errors: "U" for units can be read as a zero, "QD" and "QOD" are confused, "MS" could mean morphine sulfate or magnesium sulfate, a trailing zero after a decimal point can be misread as a tenfold larger amount, and a missing leading zero before a decimal point can be missed entirely. Write the full word when in doubt.

Third, context-dependent abbreviations. "MS" can be multiple sclerosis, mitral stenosis or mental status; "PE" can be pulmonary embolism or physical exam. Read the specialty and context before assuming.

Fourth, patient language. Terminology is for colleagues; patients need plain words. Saying "your MI" to a frightened patient communicates nothing. Teach-back, asking the patient to explain it in their own words, catches misunderstanding.

Finally, the ileum/ilium, perineal/peroneal and hypo/hyper pairs are classic dictation and handwriting traps. Good clinicians spell out laterality ("left") instead of abbreviating it, especially on consent forms and surgical sites, where wrong-site surgery is a never event.

keyPoints: Most terms = prefix + root + combining vowel + suffix; read from the suffix back.
-itis = inflammation, -ectomy = removal, -otomy = incision, -ostomy = new opening, -plasty = repair.
tachy- = fast, brady- = slow, hyper- = too much, hypo- = too little, dys- = abnormal.
Organs often have Greek and Latin roots used in different words (nephr- vs ren-).
Hematemesis = vomiting blood; hemoptysis = coughing up blood.
Dangerous abbreviations (U, QD, MS, trailing zeros) are on "Do Not Use" lists.

examples.tr: chole (bile) + cyst (bladder) + ectomy (removal) = removal of the gallbladder
thorac (chest) + centesis (puncture to remove fluid) = draining fluid from the chest

test.q: What does the suffix -ectomy mean?
test.explain: -ectomy means cutting out (excision). -itis is inflammation, -otomy is cutting into, -megaly is enlargement.

test.q: "Bradycardia" means:
test.explain: brady- = slow, cardi = heart. A fast rate would be tachycardia.

test.q: Which term means coughing up blood?
test.explain: Hemoptysis comes from the lungs/airway. Hematemesis is vomiting blood, hematuria is blood in urine, hemarthrosis is blood in a joint.

test.q: A colostomy is:
choices: A surgically created opening from the colon to the skin
Viewing the colon with a scope
test.explain: -ostomy = creating an opening (stoma). Removal would be colectomy; viewing is colonoscopy.

test.q: Which root refers to the kidney?
test.explain: Nephr- (Greek) and ren- (Latin) both mean kidney. Hepat = liver, pneum = lung/air, oste = bone.

test.q: Which -oma is NOT a tumor?
test.explain: A hematoma is a collection of blood. Lipoma, adenoma and meningioma are tumors (all usually benign).

test.q: "Neutropenia" means:
test.explain: -penia = deficiency. An excess would be neutrophilia.

test.q: What is the difference between hemiparesis and hemiplegia?
choices: Paresis is weakness; plegia is complete paralysis
Paresis is paralysis; plegia is weakness
test.explain: -paresis = partial weakness, -plegia = paralysis. hemi- = one side of the body.

test.q: Why is "U" for units on "Do Not Use" lists?
choices: It can be misread as a zero or a number, causing big errors
It is too long to write
test.explain: A handwritten U can look like 0 or 4, leading to large overdoses. Write "units" in full.

test.q: Which suffix means inflammation?
test.explain: Gastritis, hepatitis, appendicitis: -itis = inflammation.

test.q: Hepato___ means an enlarged liver.
test.explain: -megaly = enlargement, so hepatomegaly = enlarged liver.

test.q: Write the medical term for vomiting blood.
test.explain: hemat (blood) + emesis (vomiting). British spelling haematemesis.

test.q: Difficulty or abnormal breathing is called ___.
test.explain: dys- (difficult/abnormal) + pnea (breathing). British spelling dyspnoea.

kidTest.q: What does "cardi" mean?
kidTest.explain: Cardi means heart, like in cardiology, the study of the heart.

kidTest.q: "Tachy" means:
kidTest.explain: Tachy means fast. Tachycardia is a fast heartbeat.

kidTest.q: If something ends in "-itis", it is:
kidTest.explain: -itis means inflamed: red, swollen and sore.

kidTest.q: Gastritis is a sore...
kidTest.explain: Gastr means stomach (tummy) and -itis means sore and swollen.

kidTest.q: Fast is "tachy". What word part means slow?
kidTest.explain: Brady means slow, like bradycardia, a slow heartbeat.

advancedTest.q: A note says "hyperplasia" in one place and "hyperplasty" in another. Which is a real pathology term and what does it mean?
choices: Hyperplasia: an increase in cell number
Hyperplasia: an increase in cell size
advancedTest.explain: -plasia = growth/formation; hyperplasia is more cells. Increased cell size is hypertrophy. -plasty is surgical repair and "hyperplasty" is not a standard term.

advancedTest.q: Which pair is a classic dictation/handwriting trap because they name different structures?
advancedTest.explain: Ileum is the last part of the small bowel; ilium is the pelvic bone. One letter separates a bowel surgery from a hip operation.

advancedTest.q: A neurology note reads "MS normal." What is the best response?
choices: Clarify, because MS can mean mental status, multiple sclerosis or mitral stenosis
Assume multiple sclerosis has been ruled out
advancedTest.explain: Context-dependent abbreviations are a known error source; ask or read context rather than guessing.

advancedTest.q: Removing fluid from the abdomen with a needle is called para___.
advancedTest.explain: -centesis = puncture to remove fluid. Paracentesis drains ascites.

lessons.title: Anatomical Terms and Directions

levels.kid:
Doctors need a way to say exactly where something is on your body, so everyone means the same spot.

First, they imagine you standing up straight, facing them, with your hands at your sides and palms forward. That is the "starting pose."

Then they use direction words. Up toward your head is "superior." Down toward your feet is "inferior." Your belly side is the "front," and your back side is the "back." Close to your middle is "medial," and out toward your sides is "lateral."

And "left" always means YOUR left, not the doctor's left. That way, nobody gets mixed up!
levels.hs:
Anatomy uses a shared map so that "the cut is on the left arm, near the elbow" means the same thing to everyone.

The map starts with the **anatomical position**: standing upright, facing forward, arms at the sides, palms facing forward, feet forward. All directions are described as if the person were in this pose, even if they are lying down.

Paired direction terms:
- **Superior / inferior**: toward the head / toward the feet.
- **Anterior (ventral) / posterior (dorsal)**: front / back.
- **Medial / lateral**: toward the midline / away from it. Your thumb is lateral to your little finger in anatomical position.
- **Proximal / distal**: closer to / farther from where a limb attaches. The elbow is proximal to the wrist.
- **Superficial / deep**: near the surface / farther inside.

Body planes are imaginary slices:
- **Sagittal**: splits left from right.
- **Coronal (frontal)**: splits front from back.
- **Axial (transverse)**: splits top from bottom, like slices in a CT scan.

Positions: **supine** is lying face up, **prone** is lying face down.

The abdomen is divided into four quadrants: right upper, left upper, right lower, left lower. Appendicitis classically ends up in the right lower quadrant.

One golden rule: left and right are always the patient's left and right.
levels.college:
Directional terminology is defined relative to the anatomical position (upright, face and feet forward, arms by the sides, palms anterior). This matters because a supine patient's "anterior" still faces the ceiling, and a pronated forearm still has its "radial" side defined by anatomical position.

Beyond the basic pairs (superior/inferior, anterior/posterior, medial/lateral, proximal/distal, superficial/deep), clinicians use:
- **Ipsilateral / contralateral**: same side / opposite side. Essential in neurology, where a left hemisphere lesion causes contralateral (right) weakness.
- **Cranial (rostral) / caudal**: toward the head / toward the tail.
- Limb-specific terms: **palmar (volar) / dorsal** for the hand, **plantar / dorsal** for the foot, **radial / ulnar** and **tibial / fibular** for sides of the limb.

Planes and imaging: sagittal, coronal and axial planes correspond directly to MRI and CT reconstructions. A **midsagittal** plane passes exactly through the midline; parasagittal planes are parallel to it.

Abdominal mapping uses either four quadrants or nine regions: right and left hypochondriac, epigastric, right and left lumbar (flanks), umbilical, right and left iliac (inguinal), and hypogastric (suprapubic). Pain location in these regions narrows the differential: epigastric pain suggests stomach, pancreas or even the heart; right hypochondriac pain suggests gallbladder or liver.

Motion terms include flexion/extension, abduction (away from midline)/adduction (toward midline), internal/external rotation, and pronation/supination. Deformity terms are notorious: **varus** means the distal segment angles toward the midline (genu varum = bow legs), and **valgus** means it angles away (genu valgum = knock knees).
levels.phd:
Anatomical terminology encodes a coordinate system, and its subtleties appear wherever the body plan is not a simple cylinder.

The central nervous system is the best example. In a fish or a four-legged animal, the neuraxis is straight, so dorsal means "toward the back" everywhere. In humans the axis bends roughly at the midbrain–diencephalon junction because we stand upright. Below the bend (brainstem and spinal cord), dorsal equals posterior and rostral equals superior. Above it (forebrain), dorsal equals superior and rostral equals anterior. Hence the "dorsal" surface of the spinal cord faces your back, while the "dorsal" surface of the cerebrum faces the ceiling. Neuroscience papers using rodent data depend on this mapping.

The terms are standardized by Terminologia Anatomica, curated by the Federative International Programme for Anatomical Terminology, which replaced eponyms with descriptive Latin terms where possible, though clinicians still use many eponyms.

Development explains several confusing conventions. The upper and lower limbs rotate in opposite directions during embryogenesis: the upper limb rotates laterally and the lower limb medially. That is why the thumb is lateral but the big toe is medial, and why the extensor compartment of the leg faces anteriorly. It also explains the spiral pattern of lower limb dermatomes.

Imaging conventions add another layer. Axial CT and MRI are, by convention, displayed as if viewed from the patient's feet, so the patient's right appears on the viewer's left. Coronal images are displayed as if facing the patient. Misunderstanding these conventions has contributed to laterality errors.

Finally, "varus" and "valgus" are defined by the direction of the distal segment, which is why some historic texts used them inconsistently; the modern convention is unambiguous only when the joint is named.
levels.expert:
In practice, anatomical language is a safety system, and the high-stakes failure is laterality.

Wrong-site surgery is a "never event," and the Universal Protocol exists because of it: verifying the procedure and site, marking the site with the surgeon's initials while the patient is awake and can confirm, and a time-out before incision. Write "left" and "right" in full on consents and notes, and never mark the non-operative side.

Imaging laterality errors are common teaching cases: axial images display the patient's right on the viewer's left. Always check the side marker on a radiograph, and remember that a portable film can be flipped.

In notes, describe findings so a stranger could locate them: "2 cm laceration over the dorsal aspect of the left hand, proximal to the 3rd metacarpophalangeal joint." Use clock-face descriptions for wounds and breast findings, and dermatomal or surface-landmark language for neurological findings.

In neurology, ipsilateral and contralateral drive localization: a right-sided facial droop plus right arm weakness points to the left hemisphere, whereas a right facial weakness with left limb weakness ("crossed" signs) suggests a brainstem lesion. The words carry the reasoning.

Orthopedists will quiz you on varus and valgus: the name describes where the distal segment points relative to midline. Genu valgum is knock-kneed; a valgus stress test of the knee opens the medial side and tests the medial collateral ligament.

For abdominal pain, use the nine-region language and remember referred pain: early appendicitis often starts periumbilical before migrating to the right lower quadrant, and inferior myocardial infarction can present as epigastric pain.

keyPoints: All directions assume anatomical position: upright, facing forward, palms forward.
Proximal/distal = nearer/farther from a limb's attachment; medial/lateral = toward/away from midline.
Sagittal splits left/right, coronal splits front/back, axial splits top/bottom.
Supine = face up; prone = face down.
Left and right always mean the patient's; axial scans show patient's right on viewer's left.
Varus = distal part angled toward midline (bow legs); valgus = away (knock knees).

examples.src: The wrist is distal to the elbow.
examples.tr: Distal = farther from the limb's attachment at the shoulder.

examples.src: A left hemisphere stroke causes right-sided weakness.
examples.tr: Contralateral: motor pathways cross, so the deficit is on the opposite side.

test.q: In anatomical position, the palms face:
test.explain: Anatomical position has palms facing forward (anteriorly).

test.q: The knee is ___ to the ankle.
test.explain: The knee is closer to the hip (the limb's attachment), so it is proximal to the ankle.

test.q: Which plane divides the body into front and back?
test.explain: Coronal (frontal) separates anterior from posterior. Sagittal separates left/right; axial separates top/bottom.

test.q: A patient lying face down is:
test.explain: Prone = face down. Supine = face up (think "on your spine").

test.q: In anatomical position, the thumb is ___ to the little finger.
test.explain: Palms forward puts the thumb on the outside, so it is lateral.

test.q: On a standard axial CT image, the patient's right side appears:
test.explain: Axial images are viewed as if from the patient's feet, so patient right is on the viewer's left.

test.q: Pain in the right upper quadrant most suggests a problem with the:
test.explain: Liver and gallbladder sit in the RUQ. Spleen is LUQ, appendix RLQ, sigmoid LLQ.

test.q: Knock knees are called:
test.explain: Valgus = distal segment angled away from midline, producing knock knees. Varum is bow-legged.

test.q: A left cerebral lesion causing right arm weakness is described as:
test.explain: The weakness is on the opposite side of the lesion: contralateral.

test.q: What word means lying face up?
test.explain: Supine = face up, on the back. Prone = face down.

test.q: Toward the midline is called ___.
test.explain: Medial = toward the midline; lateral = away from it.

test.q: Which plane divides the body into left and right parts?
test.explain: Sagittal planes run front-to-back and separate left from right; midsagittal is exactly central.

test.q: The palm side of the hand is called the palmar or ___ surface.
test.explain: Volar = palmar. The back of the hand is the dorsal surface.

kidTest.q: When a doctor says "left", whose left is it?
kidTest.explain: Left always means the patient's left, so nobody gets mixed up.

kidTest.q: "Superior" means closer to your:
kidTest.explain: Superior means up, toward the head.

kidTest.q: Which part is the front of your body?
kidTest.explain: The belly side is the front (anterior).

kidTest.q: In the starting pose, your palms face:
kidTest.explain: In anatomical position, palms face forward.

kidTest.q: Down toward your feet is called "in___" (finish the word).
kidTest.explain: Inferior means lower, toward the feet.

kidTest.q: "Lateral" means:
kidTest.explain: Lateral means away from the middle, out to the side.

advancedTest.q: In the forebrain, the "dorsal" surface faces:
choices: Superiorly, toward the top of the head
advancedTest.explain: The human neuraxis bends at the midbrain–diencephalon junction, so in the forebrain dorsal = superior, while in the spinal cord dorsal = posterior.

advancedTest.q: A valgus stress applied to the knee primarily tests the:
advancedTest.explain: Valgus stress pushes the knee inward and the leg outward, opening the medial joint line and loading the MCL.

advancedTest.q: Why is the big toe medial while the thumb is lateral?
choices: The lower limb lacks a radial side
It is just convention with no basis
The foot is always held pronated
The limbs rotate in opposite directions during development
advancedTest.explain: In embryogenesis the upper limb rotates laterally and the lower limb medially, so the preaxial digit ends up lateral in the hand and medial in the foot.

advancedTest.q: Right facial weakness with LEFT arm and leg weakness most suggests a lesion in the:
advancedTest.explain: "Crossed" findings (cranial nerve deficit on one side, limb weakness on the other) localize to the brainstem.

lessons.title: The SOAP Note

levels.kid:
When a doctor sees you, they write a little story about your visit so other doctors can read it later. Many doctors write it in four parts called SOAP, like soap for washing!

- **S** is for what YOU say: "My ear hurts."
- **O** is for what the doctor sees and measures: a red ear and a temperature.
- **A** is for what the doctor thinks is wrong: an ear infection.
- **P** is for the plan: medicine and rest.

Writing it the same way every time helps every doctor find things fast, like a well-organized backpack.
levels.hs:
Doctors document every visit. One of the most common formats is the **SOAP note**, which keeps notes organized so any clinician can quickly understand what happened.

- **S: Subjective.** What the patient (or family) reports. This includes the chief complaint in the patient's words ("I've had a cough for a week"), the story of the illness, and relevant history such as past illnesses, medicines, allergies and family history.
- **O: Objective.** What can be observed or measured: vital signs, physical exam findings, lab results and imaging.
- **A: Assessment.** The doctor's interpretation: the most likely diagnosis and other possibilities, with the reasoning that links S and O together.
- **P: Plan.** What happens next: tests to order, treatments, patient education, and follow-up.

A simple rule helps you sort information: if the patient told you, it's S; if you measured or saw it, it's O. "Patient says she had a fever" is subjective; "Temperature 38.6 °C" is objective.

Good notes matter because medicine is a team sport. The night doctor, a specialist, or the same doctor next month all rely on the note. Notes are also legal records, and patients can often read their own notes, so they should be accurate, respectful and clear.
levels.college:
The SOAP note originated with Lawrence Weed's problem-oriented medical record (POMR) in the late 1960s, which reorganized charts around a numbered problem list rather than a chronological narrative.

**Subjective** contains the chief complaint, the history of present illness (HPI, often structured with onset, location, duration, character, aggravating/alleviating factors, radiation, timing and severity), review of systems (ROS), past medical and surgical history, medications, allergies (with the reaction), family and social history.

**Objective** contains vital signs, the physical exam by system, and data: labs, imaging, ECG, and results of procedures. Only verifiable findings belong here.

**Assessment** is where the clinician thinks on paper. A strong assessment opens with a one-line summary ("62-year-old man with diabetes presenting with 2 hours of exertional chest pressure and inferior ST elevation"), then names the leading diagnosis, the important alternatives, and the evidence for and against each.

**Plan** is organized by problem, and each problem gets its own diagnostics, therapeutics, monitoring, patient education, and disposition (admit, discharge, follow-up).

In hospitals, the daily progress note is usually written as "Assessment and Plan by problem": #1 community-acquired pneumonia, #2 acute kidney injury, #3 diabetes, each with its own mini-plan. A variant, the APSO note, puts assessment and plan first because they are what readers want most.

Common errors: putting patient-reported information in O, writing an assessment that just restates data without interpretation, and plans that are vague ("monitor") without saying what will be monitored and what will trigger action.
levels.phd:
The SOAP structure embodies an epistemology. Weed argued that the medical record should expose the clinician's reasoning to scrutiny, the way a scientific paper exposes its methods. Separating subjective report from objective observation, then explicitly stating inferences (assessment) and actions (plan), makes it possible to audit whether conclusions followed from data.

That ideal has been strained by the electronic health record. Templates, auto-populated data and copy-forward features produce "note bloat": progress notes dominated by pasted lab tables and outdated text. Studies of EHR notes have found that a large share of text in many progress notes is copied or imported rather than newly written, and copied errors propagate across days. Because notes are also billing documents, documentation has been shaped by coding requirements, not just clinical communication.

The subjective/objective division is itself philosophically imperfect. A pain score is a measured number but a subjective experience; an exam finding such as "mild tenderness" depends on observer judgment, and inter-rater reliability for many signs is modest. The categories are better seen as "reported" versus "examiner-generated."

Policy has changed the audience. Open-notes programs and, in the United States, the information-blocking provisions of the 21st Century Cures Act mean patients can usually read their notes promptly. Research on open notes found patients reported better understanding and adherence, while clinicians adjusted language, for instance avoiding stigmatizing words such as "noncompliant" or "denies" in favor of neutral phrasing.

Finally, notes are increasingly read by machines. Natural language processing extracts problems, phenotypes and outcomes from free text, so the structure and precision of the note now influence research datasets and decision-support tools as well as patient care.
levels.expert:
Attendings read your note to answer one question: does this person understand what is going on with the patient and what to do next?

Practical rules:

- **Lead the assessment with a one-liner** that contains age, key risk factors, the presenting problem and the most important data. A good one-liner is the diagnosis's illness script in miniature.
- **Commit.** "Chest pain, will work up" is not an assessment. "Likely unstable angina given exertional pattern and risk factors; less likely PE (no tachycardia, Wells low); aortic dissection unlikely (no tearing pain, equal pulses)" shows reasoning and names the can't-miss alternatives.
- **Plan by problem with explicit triggers**: "Repeat troponin in 3 hours; if rising, call cardiology" beats "trend troponin."
- **Code status, allergies with reactions, and disposition** belong in every admission note. "Penicillin: hives" and "penicillin: anaphylaxis" lead to different decisions.

Medicolegally, the standard is "if it wasn't documented, it wasn't done." Document informed consent discussions, what you told the patient, and return precautions. Late entries are labeled as late, never backdated; never alter a note after an adverse event except through a dated addendum.

Avoid copy-forward rot: a "no edema" copied for four days in a patient now with leg swelling is a liability and a safety problem. Delete stale text.

Use respectful language because patients read notes: "reports" rather than "claims," "declined" rather than "refused," and describe behaviors rather than labeling the person.

In neurosurgery, the notes are short and serial: daily neuro exam (GCS components, pupils, motor strength by limb), drain output, wound check. The trend matters more than the single exam, so be precise enough that tomorrow's resident can tell whether the patient changed.

keyPoints: SOAP = Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan.
Patient-reported = Subjective; measured or observed = Objective.
The assessment interprets data: leading diagnosis, alternatives and reasoning.
The plan is organized by problem: diagnostics, treatment, education, disposition.
Developed from Lawrence Weed's problem-oriented medical record (late 1960s).
Copy-forward errors and vague plans are common documentation pitfalls.

examples.src: S: "Burning when I pee for 2 days." O: T 38.1 °C, suprapubic tenderness, urinalysis positive for nitrites. A: Acute cystitis. P: Urine culture, antibiotic, fluids, return if flank pain or vomiting.
examples.tr: A miniature SOAP note: report, findings, interpretation, plan.

test.q: What does the O in SOAP stand for?
test.explain: O = Objective: measurable or observable data such as vitals, exam and test results.

test.q: "The patient says she had a fever last night" belongs in which section?
test.explain: It is reported by the patient, not measured by the clinician, so it is Subjective.

test.q: A blood pressure reading belongs in:
test.explain: A measured vital sign is Objective data.

test.q: Which section contains the clinician's interpretation and differential diagnosis?
test.explain: The Assessment interprets the data, names the likely diagnosis and alternatives.

test.q: Who developed the problem-oriented medical record from which SOAP notes come?
test.explain: Lawrence Weed introduced the problem-oriented medical record in the late 1960s.

test.q: Which is the best-written plan item?
choices: Repeat potassium in the morning; if low, replace and recheck
test.explain: Good plans are specific and say what triggers action. Vague words like "monitor" are not plans.

test.q: Why should allergies be documented with the reaction?
choices: The type of reaction (rash vs anaphylaxis) changes clinical decisions
It is required for billing only
So the patient can read it
test.explain: A mild rash and anaphylaxis carry very different risks and lead to different choices.

test.q: In a hospital progress note, the assessment and plan are usually organized:
choices: By which nurse is on shift
test.explain: Problem-based assessment and plan (#1, #2, #3) keeps each issue's reasoning and actions together.

test.q: What is "copy-forward" error?
choices: Pasting old text into new notes so outdated findings appear current
Copying a note to a specialist
test.explain: Copied text can carry outdated or wrong findings forward day after day.

test.q: What does the P in SOAP stand for?
test.explain: P = Plan: tests, treatments, education and follow-up.

test.q: The chief complaint and history of present illness go in the ___ section.
test.explain: They are the patient's report, so they are Subjective.

test.q: Name the SOAP variant that puts assessment and plan first.
test.explain: APSO reorders the note so the most-read parts (assessment and plan) come first.

test.q: Lab results and imaging findings belong in the ___ section.
test.explain: Test results are verifiable data, so they go in Objective.

kidTest.q: What does the S in a SOAP note stand for?
kidTest.explain: S is Subjective: what you tell the doctor.

kidTest.q: A thermometer shows you have a fever. Which part is that?
kidTest.explain: O is for what the doctor sees and measures.

kidTest.q: The "P" part tells:
choices: The plan to help you get better
kidTest.explain: P is the plan: medicine, rest and checkups.

kidTest.q: Why do doctors write notes the same way every time?
choices: So others can find things fast
kidTest.explain: Same order every time means any doctor can read it quickly.

kidTest.q: How many parts does a SOAP note have? (write the number)
kidTest.explain: S, O, A and P: four parts.

advancedTest.q: Which assessment best shows clinical reasoning?
choices: Chest pain, will rule out everything.
Likely unstable angina given exertional pattern and risk factors; PE less likely (no tachycardia, low Wells score); dissection unlikely (equal pulses, no tearing pain).
advancedTest.explain: A strong assessment commits to a leading diagnosis and explains why key dangerous alternatives are more or less likely.

advancedTest.q: After an adverse event, a resident realizes an earlier note was incomplete. The correct action is:
choices: Write a clearly dated late-entry addendum
Ask the nurse to rewrite it
Edit the original note so it looks complete
advancedTest.explain: Records are never altered retroactively; corrections are made by dated, labeled addenda.

advancedTest.q: Why is the strict subjective/objective split philosophically imperfect?
choices: Some "objective" findings depend on examiner judgment and some measured numbers record subjective experience
Exam findings are always fully objective
advancedTest.explain: Pain scores are numbers recording an experience, and signs like "mild tenderness" vary between examiners, so the split is better described as reported versus examiner-generated.

lessons.title: Presenting a Patient

levels.kid:
In a hospital, doctors work as a team. When one doctor meets a new patient, they tell the rest of the team about that person. This is called presenting.

They tell it like a short, clear story in the same order every time: who the patient is, why they came, what has been happening, what the doctor found, and what the plan is.

It's like telling your friend about a movie: you don't tell every tiny detail, just the important parts, in order, so they understand. A good presentation helps the whole team help the patient faster.
levels.hs:
On hospital rounds, students and residents give **oral case presentations**: a short spoken summary that lets the team understand a patient quickly. It follows a standard order:

1. **Identification and chief complaint**: "Mr. A is a 58-year-old man with high blood pressure who presents with chest pain for 3 hours."
2. **History of present illness**: the story, in time order, with details that matter.
3. **Past history, medications, allergies, social and family history**: only what's relevant.
4. **Exam**: vital signs first, then key findings.
5. **Data**: important labs and imaging.
6. **Assessment and plan**: a one-sentence summary, the most likely diagnosis, alternatives, and next steps.

Two ideas make presentations good:
- **Pertinent positives**: findings that support a diagnosis (crushing chest pain spreading to the left arm).
- **Pertinent negatives**: important things that are absent and help rule out alternatives (no fever, no leg swelling).

A new patient presentation is usually only a few minutes long, so you have to choose. Saying "no headache" in a chest pain case wastes time; saying "no shortness of breath" might matter.

Doctors also hand patients over at shift change. Short structured formats such as **SBAR** (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) make sure nothing important is forgotten.
levels.college:
An oral presentation is an argument, not a transcript. Its purpose is to lead the listener to the same assessment you reached, so every included detail should either support your leading diagnosis, argue against an alternative, or affect management.

Structure for a new admission:
- **Opening line**: age, sex, relevant background, chief complaint and duration.
- **HPI**: chronological, integrating pertinent positives and negatives from the review of systems. Relevant risk factors (smoking for chest pain, travel for fever) belong here, not buried later.
- **Brief PMH, meds, allergies, social history**.
- **Exam**: vitals with trends, general appearance, then focused systems; report findings, not maneuvers ("lungs with crackles at the right base," not "I listened to the lungs").
- **Data**: abnormal or decision-relevant results, with comparison to baseline where available.
- **Assessment and plan**: one-line summary, prioritized problem list, differential with reasoning, and a plan for each problem.

Follow-up presentations on rounds are shorter and organized as interval events, today's exam and data, then assessment and plan by problem.

Handoffs are a distinct skill. Communication failures are a leading contributor to serious adverse events. **SBAR** is used widely, especially for urgent nurse-to-physician communication. **I-PASS** (Illness severity, Patient summary, Action list, Situation awareness and contingency planning, Synthesis by receiver) was tested in a multicenter study of pediatric residency programs and was associated with fewer medical errors and about 30 percent fewer preventable adverse events, without longer handoffs.

Common errors include burying the chief complaint, presenting labs without interpretation, and giving a differential that does not match the history you just told.
levels.phd:
The case presentation is a genre with its own rhetoric, and educators have studied it as a window into clinical reasoning.

Research on oral presentations shows that attendings and students often have different implicit goals: students tend to aim for completeness to demonstrate diligence, while attendings value selection and synthesis as evidence of reasoning. Lingard and colleagues described how students learn the presentation as a performance of competence, including how to express uncertainty without appearing unprepared.

The presentation also serves as a form of "thinking out loud." Choosing which details to include requires the presenter to have an active hypothesis, which is why the structure aligns with illness scripts: predisposing factors (in the opening line), the temporal pattern and features (HPI), and consequences (exam and data). Feedback models such as the One-Minute Preceptor ("get a commitment, probe for supporting evidence, teach a general rule, reinforce what was done right, correct mistakes") use the presentation to expose reasoning.

At the systems level, handoff science treats verbal transfer as a high-risk event. Studies of sentinel events have repeatedly identified communication breakdown as a major contributing factor. Structured tools reduce omission, and the synthesis or read-back step closes the loop by verifying that the receiver's mental model matches the sender's. I-PASS added a written component and contingency planning, which addresses the fact that the overnight clinician must anticipate deterioration rather than just know the current state.

Cognitive load theory offers a reason structure helps: a predictable order frees working memory for content. However, rigid templates can encourage rote recitation. The best presentations are structured but tailored, a balance that is hard to teach explicitly and is learned mostly through feedback.
levels.expert:
What attendings listen for in the first 30 seconds: Do you know why the patient is here, how sick they are, and what you think is going on?

Practical craft:
- **Front-load severity.** If the patient is unstable, say so first: "I'm worried about this patient; she's hypotensive despite fluids." Don't make the team wait through the social history.
- **Make the one-liner do the work.** "A 72-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation not on anticoagulation, presenting with sudden right arm weakness and aphasia, last known well 50 minutes ago" already tells the team this is a stroke code with a time-critical decision.
- **Interpret numbers.** "Creatinine 2.1, up from a baseline of 0.9" is information; "creatinine 2.1" is a puzzle for the listener.
- **Match the differential to the story.** If you mention pulmonary embolism, the HPI should already have told us about leg swelling, immobility or recent surgery, positive or negative.
- **Own a plan.** Even if it is wrong, a committed plan lets the attending teach. "I don't know" is acceptable for facts; it is not acceptable for what you would do next.
- **Say what you are worried about.** Contingency statements ("If her pressure drops below X, I would...") are the core of a safe handoff.

In neurosurgery and other surgical fields, presentations are compressed: neuro exam, imaging, drains, wound, plan. Surgeons want laterality, GCS components and pupil findings precisely and fast.

For handoffs, use I-PASS or your institution's tool every time, include the receiver's read-back, and never hand off a pending critical result without saying who will act on it.

keyPoints: Order: ID and chief complaint, HPI, PMH/meds/allergies/social, exam, data, assessment and plan.
Pertinent positives support your diagnosis; pertinent negatives argue against alternatives.
A presentation is an argument for your assessment, not a list of everything.
Interpret data (compare with baseline) rather than reading numbers.
SBAR = Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation.
I-PASS handoffs were linked to fewer errors and preventable adverse events.

examples.src: "Ms. B is a 34-year-old woman on oral contraceptives presenting with 1 day of pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath. She has a swollen left calf and a heart rate of 118."
examples.tr: A strong opening: risk factor, symptoms and the key signs that point toward pulmonary embolism.

test.q: Which item comes first in a standard oral case presentation?
test.explain: The opening line gives who the patient is and why they came.

test.q: A pertinent negative is:
choices: An absent finding that helps rule out an important alternative
A finding that confirms the diagnosis
test.explain: Pertinent negatives are absent findings that matter for the differential (e.g. no leg swelling when considering PE).

test.q: In a chest pain presentation, which detail is most pertinent?
choices: The patient had chickenpox at age 6
Pain radiates to the left arm with sweating
test.explain: Radiation to the arm with diaphoresis supports acute coronary syndrome.

test.q: What does SBAR stand for?
test.explain: SBAR structures urgent communication, often between nurses and physicians.

test.q: Which is the better way to report a lab?
test.explain: Comparing with baseline interprets the number and shows an acute change.

test.q: When should you say a patient is unstable during a presentation?
test.explain: Severity is front-loaded so the team can act.

test.q: What does the S in I-PASS stand for (the last letter)?
test.explain: I-PASS: Illness severity, Patient summary, Action list, Situation awareness and contingency planning, Synthesis by receiver.

test.q: Why is reporting "I listened to the lungs" weaker than "crackles at the right base"?
choices: It is in the wrong section
It describes the maneuver, not the finding
test.explain: Present findings, not actions.

test.q: A presenter mentions aortic dissection in the differential but said nothing about the pain's character or pulses. What's the problem?
choices: The differential isn't supported by the history and exam presented
Pulses are not part of the exam
test.explain: The story must already include the pertinent positives/negatives for each alternative you raise.

test.q: What does the R in SBAR stand for?
test.explain: SBAR ends with what you want done: the recommendation.

test.q: Absent findings that help rule out alternatives are called pertinent ___.
test.explain: Pertinent negatives argue against competing diagnoses.

test.q: In SBAR, what does the B stand for?
test.explain: Background: the relevant history and context.

test.q: The final step of I-PASS, where the receiver repeats back the key points, is synthesis by ___.
test.explain: Synthesis by receiver closes the communication loop.

kidTest.q: What is presenting a patient?
choices: Telling the team about a patient
kidTest.explain: Presenting means telling the team the patient's story.

kidTest.q: A good presentation is like:
choices: Telling a friend the important parts of a movie, in order
kidTest.explain: Short, clear, in order, with the important parts.

kidTest.q: What comes at the end of a presentation?
kidTest.explain: The plan is what the team will do next.

kidTest.q: Why do doctors present patients?
choices: So the team can help faster
kidTest.explain: Sharing the story helps the whole team help the patient.

kidTest.q: Doctors work together as a ___ (one word, rhymes with "seam").
kidTest.explain: Doctors work as a team, so they share what they know.

advancedTest.q: Which opening line best signals a time-critical decision?
choices: "A 72-year-old woman with AF not anticoagulated, sudden right arm weakness and aphasia, last known well 50 minutes ago."
"A 72-year-old woman admitted for weakness, here is her social history."
advancedTest.explain: Age, risk factor, focal deficit and last-known-well time immediately frame an acute stroke treatment decision.

advancedTest.q: What element of I-PASS specifically addresses overnight deterioration?
advancedTest.explain: Contingency planning gives the receiver if/then actions for anticipated changes.

advancedTest.q: In the One-Minute Preceptor model, what is the first step after a learner presents?
advancedTest.explain: The preceptor first asks the learner to commit to a diagnosis or plan, which exposes their reasoning.
